idiom_name: flags struct / func() bool gate, loaded with os.Getenv; //go:build for compile-time
implementation_notes: Go has no router abstraction and needs none: read the flag once at start-up (os.Getenv, the flag package or a config file), keep it in a Flags struct or expose it as a method, and inject that value into the types that need it so the toggle point is a plain boolean read. Compile-time selection is the build system's job - a //go:build constraint keeps the gated file out of the compilation entirely, which is how Go expresses build-time features. Reach for a real provider (the OpenFeature Go SDK, or a flag service behind an interface) only when flags need targeting, cohorts, an audit trail or an administrative UI; for a handful of release flags the struct field is the honest implementation.
pitfalls: Calling os.Getenv at every toggle point hides the dependency from tests and re-reads the environment on each request; load once and inject.
A Flags struct copied by value gives each goroutine a private snapshot: if flags must be flipped at runtime, guard the field with sync/atomic or a mutex, or the reload is invisible.
//go:build constraints split the build matrix; a tag-guarded file is never compiled in CI unless a build job passes that tag.
Comparing the environment value to "1" is only safe if the convention is enforced; os.Getenv returns "" for an unset variable, so "false" and "unset" behave identically.
